main_point.en: We can imitate Jesus and pray honestly and faithfully, fully depending on God.

christ_connection.en: l Jesus taught us to pray with dependence on God, recognizing our physical and spiritual needs, which only He can supply; faith in God, knowing He is our good and loving Father; and with persistence, remembering He is righteous. It is through the death and resurrection of Jesus that we have access to the Father so that we can pray in faith.

content.en: 1 Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” 2 And he said to them, “When you pray, say: “Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. 3 Give us each day our daily bread, 4 and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.”

title.en: God Listens as Our Good Father

content.en: 5 And he said to them, “Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, 6 for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’; 7 and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? 8 I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. 9 And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. 10 For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. 11 What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; 12 or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? 13 If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!”
Leaders: What a privilege to teach students how to pray—how to come before our holy God, who cares and listens to their needs and who speaks to them in return, when they listen for His voice.

“Jesus ‘was praying in a certain place’ (v. 1). A disciple saw him and asked, ‘Lord, teach us to pray’ (v. 1). That request means prayer is not something learned automatically. Prayer is not natural. Effective prayer has to be taught and learned. There’s no shame in not knowing how to pray or feeling uncomfortable in prayer. There’s only shame if we don’t ask to be taught and as a result spend years of our Christian lives ineffective in prayer.”"
“It was unusual for Jews to refer to God as ‘Father.’ Such an address would seem too personal and familiar.””
“It was unusual for Jews to refer to God as ‘Father.’ Such an address would seem too personal and familiar.”¹³

title.en: God Listens as Our Good Father

content.en: “Ask’ ... ‘seek’... ‘knock’ refer to prayer and reflect the persistence theme emphasized in the story of vv. 5-8. The assurance that ‘everyone who asks receives’ does not mean that every prayer is answered as we want it to be. Rather, it means that if we persist in prayer, our prayers will eventually be answered according to God’s best for us.”

Disciples in Jesus’s day would’ve often expected, even requested, their rabbis or leaders to teach them how to pray. Knowing that John the Baptist had instructed his disciples on prayer, Jesus’s disciples wanted to hear what their teacher had to say. So, the disciples’ question wouldn’t have been unusual. The questioner could’ve been seeking specific words as an example (which is what Jesus gave here), a pattern for all prayers (which is how the Model Prayer is set up in Matt. 6), or general information on the topic of prayer. This prayer in Luke 11 may sound familiar because Jesus taught a similar prayer in Matthew 6:9-13. This is the prayer we’re more familiar with, sometimes called “the Model Prayer” or “the Lord’s Prayer.” Though scholars disagree about whether this is the same teaching, just described differently by two different Gospel writers, some believe the most likely scenario is that Jesus taught the same prayer multiple times, since He wanted His disciples to be familiar with the pattern. Using this prayer as a pattern (to move from praising God to making our own requests) and praying the specific words are acceptable ways we can apply Jesus’s teaching here.

If God is in control and already knows the future, why pray? The Bible teaches that although God has a plan for this world that He promises to fulfill, prayer is often the means God uses to accomplish His divine purpose. Even though God knows the end result, the means that lead to that end result will be accomplished through prayer. In this sense, it is true that “prayer changes things,” and it is also true that God uses prayer to change our hearts so that our will comes into conformity with His.

FATHER, YOU ARE GOOD AND YOU WANT TO HEAR OUR HEARTS. TEACH US TO PRAY SO THAT WE MAY TEACH OUR STUDENTS TO PRAY EFFECTIVELY AND PERSISTENTLY. ENCOURAGE OUR HEARTS NOT TO GIVE UP BUT TO KEEP PRAYING FOR STUDENTS WHO DON’T KNOW YOU OR HAVE WALKED AWAY FROM YOU.
Did you know the book of Psalms is made up of prayers and songs to God? The Israelites used these to worship God, and they can guide our prayers and worship too!

instructions.en:
These optional activities are designed to help your students interact. You'll find a Discussion Activity and a Cultural Connection, which touches on a relevant topic in today’s teen culture. Each group is different, so adapt these activities to fit your group’s needs. The goal is for students to connect more to the lesson as they connect to the topic and to one another.

Ask the following questions, allowing time for students to share responses:

question.en: WHAT'S THE LAST GIFT YOU RECEIVED THAT YOU'D CALL A GOOD GIFT?
WHAT MAKES SOMETHING A GOOD GIFT?

content.en: Because we’re all designed uniquely with different needs, preferences, and desires, what we view as a “good” gift might vary. But we can probably agree that a good gift—an object, a relationship, or even a solution to a problem—makes our lives better somehow. God is the ultimate Giver of good gifts, and the cool thing is He wants us to come to Him and honestly tell Him what we need.

cultural_connection.en: Sometimes, our most honest prayers are questions. Yet, some of us hesitate to come to God with our questions and requests. Isn’t it wrong to question God? Yes, but questioning God and asking God questions are two totally different things. Questioning God’s character or motives implies we think we know better or could do better; questioning His character stems from unbelief. Asking a question implies we want to know and understand God better. So, don’t be afraid to ask God hard questions—He can handle them. He even encourages us to come to Him with our biggest hurts and doubts. He is the source of all things, including knowledge and comfort. But here’s the key: Praying honestly doesn’t mean praying irreverently, or disrespectfully. Even when we’re hurting or confused, we need to remember who we’re talking to: our good, holy, and sovereign (in control of all things and all people) God. He deserves our humility, respect, and trust—no matter what.

question.en: Why do you think the disciples asked Jesus to teach them how to pray? When have you struggled with knowing how to pray or if you’re doing it right?

answer.en: Leaders: Share context on model prayers. We overcomplicate it, but the truth is that prayer is simply communicating with God—our good, faithful, and loving Father who wants to hear from us. Instead of avoiding prayer, especially praying aloud, you can think of it as sitting down with the One who loves you unconditionally and telling Him exactly what’s on your heart. For times you feel overwhelmed or confused, Jesus gave you a model: Start by honoring God, then pray for the good of His people, and then ask God to meet physical and spiritual needs.

question.en: Where does Jesus teach us to focus our prayers? Is it okay to ask for our wants or needs? Why or why not?

answer.en: Jesus tells us to put God first in our hearts and to trust Him to provide for all of our needs (Matt. 6:33). What we put first in our hearts, we put first in our words. So, in our prayers, we focus first on praising God and seeking His will for our lives. But then Jesus teaches us to ask God to meet our physical and spiritual needs, big and small. Because Jesus restored our relationship with God, we can ask Him directly for what we need and be confident that He will provide.

question.en: Why does the way we address God matter when we pray?

answer.en: Prayer is a conversation with God, and when we pray, we should keep in mind who God is. While God is loving, compassionate, and merciful, He is also all-powerful (omnipotent), just, and holy. And only because of Jesus can we come to Him in prayer. Our words and attitude before God should be respectful and humble, but prayer is also personal. This is why Jesus taught His disciples to address God as Father. Not only does this name remind believers we’re part of God’s family, but it also reassures us that God is not some far off, uncaring being who’s constantly disappointed in us and waiting for us to mess up. No, He is our good and loving Father, who invites us to come near with boldness and confidence, resting in His presence and asking for whatever we need (Heb. 4:16), while also respecting His holiness.

title.en: God Listens As Our Good Father

question.en: When have you served or given out of expectation? How is the way God gives to us different?

answer.en: The man in Jesus’s story would’ve given out of a sense of honor and because his friend kept knocking, not necessarily because he wanted to. If a man would do that for a friend, how much more would God do for His children—children He loves and sent His own Son to die for? God wants to give us good things because He is a good Father. And He promises that we’ll find Him when we seek Him (Jer. 29:13). So, don’t hesitate. Ask God for whatever you need, and keep asking without shame or fear, trusting that He hears you and will answer in His perfect timing and according to His perfect plan.

question.en: Have you ever asked for something over and over? What do you think asking for something with “impudence” means (v. 8)?

answer.en: Sometimes we don’t ask for what we need because we feel ashamed—from not having what others have or from not being able to do something on our own. But God invites us to set aside any fear, shame, or doubt and come before Him with boldness (Heb. 4:16); He promises to meet our needs (Matt. 6:25-34). So, we can approach Him with confidence, again and again, asking, seeking, and knocking until He opens the door to answered prayer—even if He doesn’t answer the way we hoped or expected. God never gets tired of hearing from us, and praying persistently benefits us in so many ways. Every time we ask God for what we need, we get to know Him more, and we confirm our trust in Him to provide. And every answered prayer, even the one answered with a solid “no,” helps our faith grow.

question.en: Why do we struggle to trust God listens to our prayers and that His answers are sufficient?

answer.en: We can trust God listens to us and answers our prayers because He said so. While it can be hard to trust when God doesn’t answer the way we want, His “no” is still sufficient because God Himself and His plan for our lives is a much greater “yes.” He is more than sufficient to meet all our needs. But God, our good and loving Father, has given us abundantly more than we could ask for or imagine: He sealed His promises to believers with the blood of His Son, poured out for our sins, and then with the gift of the Holy Spirit, who lives within us and helps us live life God’s way. God’s answers are sufficient, because ultimately, He has answered with Himself!

question.en: What have you prayed for halfheartedly instead of with “impudence”? How can you pray honestly instead?

answer.en: We live in a world of half-hearted commitments, of “maybe” and “almost.” All too often, these words also describe our relationship with God and our prayers. But we can’t halfway follow Jesus—that’s impossible. The call to follow Jesus is a call to be all in. Our prayers should be all in, too. So, that thing you’re afraid to ask for? Request it, trusting in God’s power to provide anything, trusting that He will only answer “yes” to what’s best for you and to what aligns with His perfect plan. That person you think will never come to know Jesus? Cry out to God on his or her behalf each day, trusting He knows the best way to convict people and draw them to Himself. That relationship you worry will never be restored? Ask God to soften the person’s heart—and to soften yours. God is a God of peace and restoration, even when it seems impossible. Pray boldly, pray persistently, and watch and see how God will move.

content.en:
JEREMIAH 29:12-14a

Puzzles are meant to be, well, puzzling. Shapes and colors grow more complex as the piece count rises. Depending on what type of puzzler you are, maybe you decide to put together little sections of the puzzle off to the side; maybe you start with all the edge pieces and fill in the inside later; or maybe you work from the top to the bottom. Regardless, you'll likely come to a point where your eyes hyperfocus on that one piece you haven't been able to place yet, and you don’t give up until you find it, ignoring all the other pieces still waiting to be placed.

If we focus on the wrong things, this kind of commitment can be detrimental. But faith and godliness require our wholehearted focus—being all in, in every area of our lives. God called His people to this kind of pursuit when they were in exile. He invited them not to fix their attention on their circumstances and struggles but on Him, on His faithfulness, and on His promise to bring them home and reestablish their kingdom. Even though their situation seemed bleak and they might’ve wondered where God was in all of it, He promised, “I’m still your good and perfect God. I’m still here, and I see you.”

No matter where we find ourselves—in seasons of joy or struggle—we can find great comfort in these words. When we go looking for God and set our hearts on building a deeper relationship with Him, we will find everything we need. So, it’s not just that we can come before God with our needs but that He invites us to do so and promises to listen to us when we do.

question.en: How does this passage encourage you to come before God with your honest prayers?
What could it look like for you to pursue God with your whole heart wherever you are right now?

prayer.en: GOD, THANK YOU FOR INVITING ME TO SEEK YOU WITH MY HEART AND MY WORDS. COMFORT ME

content.en:
A theory called “six degrees of separation” suggests a chain of only six social connections separates any two people in the world. In other words, a famous person could be a friend of your best friend’s older brother’s neighbor’s sister’s dog walker. Not complicated at all, right?

Originally, only one degree of separation existed between God and people; Adam and Eve walked with Him in the garden of Eden! But after sin entered the world, God chose specific people to be mediators—those who go between two parties—between Himself and His people. These mediators were people like Moses, King David, and the prophet Elijah. After the Exodus, God also set up the office of priest. Priests were set apart by God to do God’s work. They interceded for God’s people, made offerings for them, and made sacrifices for their sins. The only access God’s people had to Him came through other imperfect humans.

Then, Jesus came. Jesus has always been God’s plan to restore our relationship with Him. Jesus is our perfect High Priest (Heb. 4:14-16), who erases the need for any other gobetweens. Through His blood on the cross, the Bible says believers were “brought near” to God Eph. 2:13). Put simply, our direct access to God has been restored through Jesus’s blood and the presence of the Holy Spirit—the very Spirit of God—within us. Nothing separates us from Jesus (Rom. 8:31-39), so we can pray with boldness, expecting to receive the mercy and grace we need (Heb. 4:16).

question.en: In your own words, what does it mean to be brought near to God?
Why do we need to remember that nothing can separate us from God? How should that influence our prayers?

prayer.en: LORD JESUS, THANK YOU FOR RESTORING OUR RELATIONSHIP WITH GOD THROUGH YOUR PERFECT SACRIFICE ON THE CROSS. SHOW ME HOW TO PRAY WITH BOLDNESS, KNOWING I HAVE DIRECT ACCESS TO GOD THROUGH YOU.

content.en:
PHILIPPIANS 4:5b; JAMES 4:8-10

Whether you’re an athlete, performer, or volunteer, you’ve probably heard the phrase: “Alright everybody, circle up.” This phrase calls the team to gather around the leader, close enough to hear any last-minute instructions or encouraging words that person has before sending the team out to play the game, perform, or start the event. Closeness allows us to hear better and be heard more clearly, and this is just as true in our relationships as it is in these team meetings.

Closeness with God is vital to our faith. Although God is always near to us, sometimes unconfessed sin gets in the way. That’s not to say our sin can separate us from God once we’re saved—nothing can separate believers from God. Once we’re in Christ, we’re covered fully and finally by His blood and righteousness (Rom. 5:9). Instead, think of this sin like sand caught up in your shoes after a day at the beach: It doesn’t keep you from walking, but it sure makes walking a lot less comfortable. Similarly, our sin affects our closeness with God, creating a distance in our relationship with Him.

So, when Scripture tells us to draw near to God, part of drawing near means confessing any sin that might be keeping us from having—or even wanting—that close relationship with Him. Drawing near to God also means spending regular time in His Word and in prayer. When we humble ourselves before God in this way, honestly confessing our sins and depending on Him to meet our every need, He meets us right then and there with His presence and provision.

question.en: Examine your heart. What sin is hindering your relationship with God right now?
How will you draw near to God this week? Why is it good to remember that He is always near and meets you where you are?

prayer.en: GOD, YOU ARE GOOD, COMPASSIONATE, AND HOLY. I WANT TO REMEMBER ALL THAT YOU ARE WHEN I COME TO YOU. I CONFESS THAT I (DESCRIBE A SPECIFIC SIN) AND RECEIVE YOUR FORGIVENESS. THANK YOU FOR BEING NEAR TO ME, ALWAYS.

content.en:
If you're upset, frustrated, anxious, or sad, the last thing you likely want to hear is the advice to just “calm down.” When people say this, you may not only feel like they’re dismissing your feelings or not caring about what you’re going through, but you’re also left with more questions—“How do I calm down?” or “Should I not care about what I’m experiencing?” The reality is that telling someone to calm down—even yourself—isn’t the best way to ease worry or anxiety. Doing so places all the power in our hands. Although the responsibility to choose our thoughts and actions lies with us, the power to change does not.

When you read the first command in Philippians 4:6, you might feel a little like you're being told to calm down. Far from being dismissive or uncaring, though, Paul’s instruction not to worry is followed up with support. He gives us the best how-to for getting rid of anxiety: prayer and gratitude. When we pray, we don’t stop caring about what happens and give up (for example, you'd still apologize to the friend you hurt but trust God with healing the relationship), but we stop worrying because we know the outcome rests in the hands of the One who created us, knows every one of our days, loves us more than we could ever imagine, and wants what’s best for us. To pray “with thanksgiving” (v. 6), then, means to pray with the confidence of someone who lives as if God has already answered. Even if He doesn’t answer our specific petitions or requests in the way we hope or expect, we can always trust Him to answer with what’s best and to give us a peace beyond our understanding. Through His presence, we can live boldly and confidently—no matter what.

God, forgive me for worrying and not trusting You to provide for me in every way. Comfort my anxious heart and show me that coming to You with my fears and worries is always better.

question.en: What steps does Paul say to take in verse 6?
How do these verses encourage you to come to God first when you’re anxious and know He will help?

prayer.en: God, forgive me for worrying and not trusting You to provide for me in every way. Comfort my anxious heart and show me that coming to You with my fears and worries is always better.

content.en:
Have you ever faced a situation where you didn’t know what to say? Maybe you studied for an English test on grammar, but then the test was on a book you were supposed to read over the weekend. Or you were giving a presentation in an after-school club, and someone asked a question you didn’t know how to answer. More seriously, maybe a friend confronted you about something you did but didn’t realize was hurtful. Or a friend experienced tragedy or loss and you were afraid of saying the wrong thing, so you said nothing at all. All of us have days when we can’t find the right words, when we’re completely speechless.

Here’s the good thing: God is prepared for this (because God is prepared for everything). God knows that we won’t always know how to ask Him for help. He knows we’ll have days that leave us speechless before Him, whether we’ve messed up or experienced something really messed up. Thankfully, one of the Holy Spirit’s roles is to pray for us when we don’t have the words. Interestingly, Scripture doesn’t say the Holy Spirit prays with normal words like we do but with “groanings too deep for words” (v. 26). The Spirit intercedes for us (goes before God on our behalf), expressing to God our needs in a language deeper than words. And God understands these groanings because He knows the Spirit’s mind.

Praying doesn’t mean you have all the right words or even realize everything that you need, but it’s an acknowledgment that, above all, you need God and trust Him to understand what you can’t even say. He knows our hearts and hears our prayers—even the ones we can’t bring ourselves to speak.

question.en: When have you struggled to know what to pray? What happened?
How are you comforted to know that the Helper God has given us (the Holy Spirit) prays for you?

prayer.en: Heavenly Father, thank You for the gift of the Holy Spirit. When I don’t have words to pray, comfort me with the truth that He prays for me, and You always hear.
